The conferees met last week and it was just a pro forma setting was all that around the horn they spent a minute or two each saying what they wanted or didn't want. It was just a formal meeting but the real stuff gets done staff and chairs and the pushback is coming of course on the work requirements for the staff program or the food staff program and the Democrats in the Senate are pushing back hard on that. the Democrats and the House are, but the votes are obviously there in the House to support work requirements because we passed it out of there. That is the biggest sticking point for a farm bill, and then should we get that resolved, then there's another big point that I think is very important to discuss, and it has real long-term implications all across this country. And that's going to be, you're expected already, Jeff, the King Amendment. or the Protect Interstate Commerce Act, which I introduced into the House version of the bill successfully in committee that passed the floor of the House for the second time in a row. And it is that we have states like California that are regulating the means and methods of production of agriculture products in other states. And so where I am right now, as we speak, I'm up in egg country. And we are, this is the number one egg producing congressional districts in America. And we have California has passed a regulation that required, first it was their producers had to double the cage size that the industry had for their laying ends. And then they realized they couldn't compete with the rest of the country. And so California passed a regulation that required any eggs being sold in California. to be certified to come from Ns that were in cages twice the industry standard size. So now we have Californian inspectors traveling into and around Iowa with their tape measures on their belt, going into our laying houses and measuring the cages and counting the Ns in each cage and deciding whether those eggs are suitable for Californians to eat. That's just one piece of this. It's also these circumstances are similar for banning gestation crates for sows for banning installs for veal cash, for denying the feeding of ducks and geese for forage or a liver. That's some of it. But the real thing is that our founding fathers established an enumerated power for Congress to regulate interstate commerce. Nobody else in the United States Congress because they wanted the states to be free trade salts. They didn't want to see that trade wars between the states. But California has already started the trade war by locking products out and specifying how they're produced. And so my legislation says this, that it bans the state from specifying and regulating the methods or means of production of agriculture products in other states. They can regulate their own producers, but they can't tell IOMs or Indians or anybody else how they're going to treat their livestock. And so that legislation needs to stay in that farm bill, if not. We're going to see all kinds of trade wars erupt between the state as the states regulate the means and methods of production of products in other states.

Well, I want to put a word of optimism in it. And I say this as I look out across a corn crop and a soybean crop that at least in my area, they'll ask me, have you ever seen a better one?
